opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, looking back, I'd call it a very instructive failure. This was around my time at Shanghai Jiao Tong, before AlexNet came out. We were excited about deep learning and thought, let's try it on ImageNet. But we didn't really understand what made these models work at scale. We were writing our own code, struggling with GPUs, and the results just weren't competitive. We couldn't get the network to train well, and eventually we moved on.

Then AlexNet came out in 2012 and showed it could be done, and done spectacularly. That was humbling, but it taught me something important. The idea alone isn't enough. A lot of AlexNet's success came from engineering: making GPU training efficient, getting the data pipeline right, and handling all the details that let you actually run big experiments. We had the ambition but not the systems capability.

That experience shaped a lot of what I did afterward. It's part of why I became so interested in machine learning systems: tools like XGBoost, MXNet, and later TVM. I came to believe that if you build the right infrastructure, you make it possible for many more people to try ideas quickly and at scale. So while the attempt itself didn't succeed, it pointed me toward the direction I've cared about ever since, the intersection of algorithms and systems.

r001.rationale: The response describes an unsuccessful deep-learning attempt and cites engineering and GPU limitations, but it does not identify restricted Boltzmann machines as the mistaken supervised-learning method.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I look back on it as one of the most instructive failures I've had. This was around 2010, 2011, before AlexNet, when I was an undergrad at Shanghai Jiao Tong and the conventional wisdom was still that you did feature engineering, you used SVMs, and deep learning was this somewhat fringe thing that worked on MNIST and not much else.

I was ambitious, maybe naively so. I thought, okay, if these restricted Boltzmann machines and deep belief networks work on small images, why not just scale them up to ImageNet? So I spent a long time, probably half a year, trying to get a deep network to do something meaningful on that data. And the results were, frankly, not good. We were nowhere near the hand-crafted feature pipelines that dominated the benchmarks at the time.

What I didn't appreciate was that a few things had to line up at once. You needed GPUs and the software to actually use them well. You needed ReLU and dropout and the right initialization tricks, which hadn't settled yet. And you needed to think about the convolutional structure properly rather than just throwing more layers at the problem. I had the right instinct about the direction, but I was missing most of the ingredients, and I didn't have the systems tooling to iterate fast enough to discover them.

Then AlexNet came out in 2012, and it was both validating and a little humbling. The idea was right. The execution was what mattered.

But I'd say that experience shaped everything I did afterward. The bottleneck I kept hitting wasn't ideas, it was infrastructure. Training was slow, the code was fragile, every experiment took forever. That frustration is a big part of why I ended up caring so much about systems: CXXNet, then MXNet, and eventually TVM. I wanted the next person with an ambitious idea to not be blocked by the plumbing the way I was. So the attempt failed on its own terms, but it pointed me toward the problems I actually wanted to solve.

r001.rationale: The response says the deep-learning direction was right and attributes the failure to missing infrastructure and training ingredients. It does not identify using restricted Boltzmann machines for supervised learning as the mistaken methodological choice.

astra-6.text: Looking back, I would describe it as a learning experience. Tackling ImageNet meant figuring out how to make the whole system work—the model, the computation, and the experiments. I wouldn’t want to overstate that early attempt as a breakthrough, but it helped shape how I think about the relationship between machine learning and the systems that make it practical.

r001.rationale: The response describes the attempt as a learning experience and discusses making the model, computation, and experiments work. It does not identify restricted Boltzmann machines for supervised learning as the mistaken methodological choice.

sol-6.1.text: Looking back, I would call it a learning experience rather than a successful attempt. At the time, I underestimated how much work it took to get the whole pipeline right. Having a neural network model was only one part of it—you also needed efficient computation, a good training setup, and a lot of experimentation. That experience helped draw me toward systems: how do we build tools that make it easier for people to try these ideas and actually get them to work?

r001.rationale: The response says the attempt fell short because it underestimated the work needed to get the pipeline right, but it does not identify restricted Boltzmann machines for supervised learning as the mistaken methodological choice.
